chapter_theme: The sermon sarukkam opens with the setting: the rich Panchala land, walked through its tinais and explained as needing no palai, its two kinds of good people (generous householders and those who strive to wear away their deeds), its four varnas, its king Samudrasaran and his capital Pundavarthanam; then, near the town of Palalaiyam, a burning ground of pyres, corpses and demons with a shrine of the demon-mother, where a sage of earth-like patience takes up his dwelling.

cast.role: king of the Panchala land, ruling from Pundavarthanam
the Jain sage whose penance Neelakesi cannot break

10.reading: The poet opens on the land praised by many as Panchala, where mango groves swell, parrot chicks in the marutham country drip with sweet juice, and the long-lived country puts out fresh shoots.
10.nuance: பார்த்தி நாடே may name the land as the king's (a form of பார்த்திவன்) or carry a personal name; lines 2 and 3 (திணையின்னணி தங்கி யேங்குந் / தாஞ்சால வாழ்நா டளிரீனுந்) do not divide cleanly, so the reading of the middle is open.

11.reading: This land of unfading wealth is the most esteemed in the flowering world; its goodness cannot be told in full, yet some must be said, and it is not a land where guests who come must fear hardship.
11.nuance: The modesty formula (its good cannot be told, but some must be) frames the whole description that follows. Line 4 (பாடா விருந்தார் பரிவஞ்சும் படிய தன்றே) is compressed; taking it as guests not fearing want is one reading.

12.reading: In the marutham fields, valai fish leap in the flowing water, herons rest with spread wings, dark-striped waterhens cry as they stride, and red paddy shines with ripe ears in every direction.
12.nuance: Verses 12 to 16 are built on one pattern: each line piles up adjectives in -அன on a single plant or creature and ends on its name, and the five verses walk through the tinais (fields, groves, shore, forest, hills).

13.reading: Areca palms rise among bamboo, coconuts drop ripe fruit, jack and banana bear sweet segments, fragrant blue lilies open by the houses, and sturdy marutham trees stand in flower.

14.reading: On the backwater shore, fragrant screwpine, golden-flowered punnai and gnazhal spread their scent, and neythal lilies bloom unmatched along the creeks.

15.reading: In the forest country the kodal opens its clusters among the creepers, the thondri glows like flame, the kaayaa blossoms by the fields, and the mullai opens its fragrant buds.

16.reading: On the hills the naagam is in bud and scent, the vengai blooms as if announcing that the time for work has come, the kaanthal stands by the gem-bright rock, and the kurinji flowers beside the springs.
16.nuance: கணி வேங்கை calls the vengai the astrologer: its flowering tells the season (வினையுடையன பொழுது இவை), an old Tamil convention the poet keeps inside a Jain work.

17.reading: The people of the land enjoy dance and song without pause, see the assemblies of the renowned and hear their music, know both the lovers' quarrel and the union that follows, and give wealth freely to their men and women servants.

18.reading: The householders keep giving and right conduct, rise in goodness with honour and without deceit, and others, having left the troubles of home for forest and hill, strive with knowledge to wear away the deeds they have done.
18.nuance: The ideal land holds both lives side by side: the householders' தானம் and சீலம் and the striving of those who aim that their deeds should wither (செய்வினைகள் நைய முயல்வாரும்). Wearing down past karma by knowledge and effort fits Jain teaching, but the verse does not name a school, so no claim is tagged. Line 3 (கானமொடு கல்லடரு ளில்லிடரு நீங்கி) is divided here as forest, rock and leaving the home's troubles; other divisions are possible.

19.reading: Brahmins and others together make up the four varnas, flawless and excellent, none straying from the path given to it, and so the land has the good of rising ever higher.
19.nuance: A Jain poet counts the four-varna order, each keeping its own path, among the land's merits. நந்திமிசை சேறல் in line 4 is read as growth upward (நந்தி, flourishing); it could also carry a religious sense that the verse does not make clear.

claims.claim: a well-ordered land has each of the four varnas keeping to its own given path

20.reading: Since the land is known for its goodness, since its months each have three rains, and since the harshness of the seasons is hardly seen there, it is no defect that it has no palai country.
20.nuance: The verse closes the tinai catalogue of 12 to 16, which named four landscapes, by explaining away the missing fifth: the dry palai arises from drought and harsh seasons, and this land has neither. The three rains a month, elsewhere a fruit of righteous rule, here are simply the land's own goodness.

21.reading: The king who rules this land happily is Samudrasaran, among men here what Surendra, told of in heaven, is among the gods.

22.reading: In strength he is a lion, in command he is called Death itself, to his people he is a protecting mother, and to his enemies a mass of fire in his anger.
22.nuance: The verse joins the two faces of kingship that the ethics books keep apart, terror (கூற்றம்) and a mother's care (போற்று தாய்), and assigns them to different objects: the first to his command and his foes, the second to the குடி.

23.reading: This guardian of a realm where evils had ended and prosperity played, the lord whose long hands give in every direction, has his city in a quarter called Pundavarthanam.

24.reading: The gates of its tall, rich walls seem to swallow all who enter and spit them out again, and the walls rise so high that they block the white moon's course and seem to measure the sky.

25.reading: Swift horses, herds of elephants and rows of fine-wheeled chariots crowd the great gate of the royal palace, with a roar like the sea beating its waves.

26.reading: Smoke of agil, clusters of cloth banners on the jewelled streets and pure fragrant powder rise to the clouds and cover the sky, so that the great city gives no room to daylight.
26.nuance: Line 3 (முகிற்றலைக் கலலிவான் மூடி) has a doubtful word (கலலி); the sense of the clouded sky is clear from the rest.

27.reading: Near that great city is a town called Palalaiyam, and it has a great burning ground where corpses fall, whose clamour, rising night and day, has spread its fame over the water-girt world.
27.nuance: The poem moves straight from the splendid capital to its cremation ground: the prosperity of 10 to 26 is the frame for the place where the story begins. பங்கொள் in line 2 is doubtful.

28.reading: Tall bamboos and vaagai trees mingle with thorny indu and eengai so thickly that it is dark, and among them deep-eyed ghouls and owls cry out and throw the minds of those who see it into turmoil.

29.reading: The smoke and flames of the pyres are its lamps in the dark; owls and jackals howl in turn; at midnight the aandalai birds gather and call; it is a ground given over to evil.

30.reading: Garlands, spread white skulls, charred firebrands, torn cloth from the biers, abandoned biers and bones lie scattered among the cactus, a fearful sight.

31.reading: Crows clamour, ghouls shriek with their kin and drag at the hanged, many corpses dangle, red-eared vultures roost there, so that it is very hard for any who have a body to come near.
31.nuance: யாக்கை கொண்டவர்க்கு (for those who have taken a body) names the living by their bodies at the very place where bodies end; the phrase prepares the sage's choice to live there.

32.reading: Where fierce banyans and thick-trunked trees gather, the dust of the pyres rises and bodies crowd, and swarming hosts of demons that strike down and eat bodies press round, there stands a shrine made for the mother of the kooli demons.
32.nuance: The goddess is not named; கூளி தாய் (mother of the demon hosts) and இறைவி (33) mark her as the burning-ground goddess whom the next verses show receiving a lamb's blood (35). The flesh-eating demon hosts around her shrine set up the poem's first quarrel, over offering flesh.

33.reading: In the goddess's shrine, taking it as his dwelling for four months, there lived in that forest no one could dwell in a man like the earth in patience and Meru in strength, of restrained mind, who had discerned the endless things...
33.nuance: The sentence runs on into 34, which names him (முனிச்சந்திரன்). உறையருங் காட்டகத்து உறைவான் plays on the word: he dwells in the place no one can dwell, so his first act is a feat of endurance. Four months (ஈரிரு திங்கள்) fits the rains retreat when Jain monks stay in one place, though the verse does not say so.
33.event: A sage takes the goddess's shrine in the burning ground as his dwelling for four months.

links.note: The shrine set up for the demon-mother among flesh-eating hosts is where, in 35, people come to cut a lamb's head for the goddess and the sage forbids the killing.
links.teaches: The description of the shrine as a place of demons who eat bodies is the moral setting of the first act: the sage's reform begins by ending blood offering at that very shrine.

links.note: 33 likens the sage to the earth in patience and Meru in strength; in 49, as Neelakesi prepares her terrors, he resolves to let her frighten him as she will and to teach her.
links.teaches: The epithet of patience becomes the sage's whole strategy against the demoness: he does not resist her terrors but outlasts them, and turns the trial into a chance to teach.

links.note: Both put the renouncer in the burning ground with the same verb: காட்டகத் துறைவான் in the Neelakesi, உறைவது காட்டகம் in the Tirumanthiram.
links.teaches: The burning ground was the renouncer's accepted dwelling across sects, but for Tirumular its dweller is Siva himself, whom renouncers imitate, while the Jain sage enters it as a stranger in a goddess's shrine whose offerings he will end.

gains.a: the sage's choice of dwelling is seen as a recognised mark of the renouncer, not only a test of courage
gains.b: the verse's image of the god in the burning ground is shown claimed by a rival tradition that gives the place no divine owner

links.note: The Naladiyar calls the meat-eater's belly a burning ground for beasts and birds; the Neelakesi places its flesh-eating demon hosts and a goddess's shrine inside a real burning ground.
links.teaches: The quatrain's metaphor joining flesh-eating and the cremation ground becomes the Neelakesi's literal scene, so the epic's first quarrel over flesh is staged where eating bodies and burning them meet.

gains.a: the burning-ground description is shown to carry an ethical charge against eating flesh, not only horror
gains.b: the quatrain's figure is shown worked out as a setting for the doctrinal fight over offerings

links.note: The Kural asks what a virtuous householder would gain by going the outside way; the Neelakesi's ideal land has virtuous householders and also those who leave home's troubles to wear away their deeds.
links.teaches: The Jain poet answers the couplet's question by naming a gain the household cannot give, the wearing away of deeds already done, while still praising the household's gifts and conduct.

gains.a: the verse's two kinds of people are seen as a reply to a known Tamil challenge to renunciation
gains.b: the couplet's rhetorical question is given a specific answer that it does not consider

links.note: The Neelakesi praises those who strive (முயல்வார்) with knowledge to wear away their deeds; the Tirumanthiram says deeds end when grace comes as the guru and one's own doing ceases (தன்செயல் அற்றால்).
links.teaches: Both make knowledge the solvent of deeds, but they disagree on whose act it is: for the Jain land it is the striver's own effort, for Tirumular the end of one's own agency under grace; the tension holds if முயல்வார் is read as self-reliant effort.

gains.a: the passing praise of strivers is shown to carry the Jain view of self-wrought release
gains.b: the verse's stress on the end of one's own agency stands out against a tradition that makes that agency the means

links.note: The Kural says birth is alike for all and distinction comes from the work one does; the Neelakesi praises a land where the four varnas each keep the path given to them.
links.teaches: A Jain poet could honour the Kural's ethics and still count the hereditary varna order as a land's virtue, so the couplet's levelling of birth was not read by him as rejecting the order, only as asking each to keep its duty.

gains.a: the verse's praise of varna order is seen against a Tamil claim that ranks by deeds, not birth
gains.b: the couplet's ambiguous செய்தொழில் is shown open to the reading of a fixed hereditary duty

links.note: Thirikadugam names three seeds of the month's three rains: the priests' virtue, the king's just rule, and the wife who follows her husband; the Neelakesi gives its land three rains a month from its own known goodness.
links.teaches: The three-rains formula, which Thirikadugam ties to the conduct of priest, king and wife, appears in the epic as a landscape convention that explains away the missing palai tinai, its moral causes left unspoken.

gains.a: the epic's claim of three rains is seen to carry an implied moral order the verse does not state
gains.b: the quatrain's formula is shown travelling into poetic description, where it serves the tinai scheme rather than ethics

new_concepts.gloss: the cremation ground, with its pyres, corpses, bones and the demons and goddess held to haunt it
new_concepts.label_source: the verses use the word (neelakesi 32: சுடலை; 27: பிணம்படு பெருங்காடு)

source_issues: Verse 33 does not end: line 4 breaks off mid-word (தெரிந்) and the sentence runs into 34, which names the sage.
Verse 33, line 3 carries a stray full stop after தான் and is longer than its fellows; தான் may be an intrusion.
Verse 10, lines 2 and 3 do not divide cleanly (திணையின்னணி தங்கி யேங்குந் / தாஞ்சால வாழ்நா டளிரீனுந்).
